intro: To rewrite a text for lower reading levels on Mac, measure the original, rewrite it in passes, then check the result against the source. A readability score gives a rough grade, not a verdict, so treat it as a flag. This page covers what the work costs, why teachers do it, free fixes that need no purchase, and where Lazur helps.
tldr: Measure the original first. A readability score gives a rough grade, not a verdict.
Rewrite in passes: meaning first, then sentences, then vocabulary.
Keep the original text and add support, such as a glossary and read-aloud, instead of only simplifying.
Check every AI rewrite line by line against the source. Studies found uneven level control and errors.
Before you paste student work into any tool, follow your school's student data rules.

blocks.text: What it costs to rewrite a text for lower reading levels

Rewriting takes longer than most people expect. You reread the original, change a sentence, reread it, then check that the change did not drop a fact. One article can take an afternoon if you do it carefully. Repeat that for several reading groups and the week runs short.

Nobody has measured how long teachers spend adapting texts, so treat any hour figure with care. A June 2025 Gallup-Walton Family Foundation survey found that teachers who use AI weekly save an average of 5.9 hours a week. Those numbers are self-reported. The survey measured general workload, not text adaptation, so use it as a hint and not a promise.

Workload also shows up in who stays. The Learning Policy Institute estimates that teacher turnover can cost nearly $25,000 per teacher in large districts, on average. Its turnover brief found a 22.0% turnover rate for teachers with low job satisfaction, against 8.0% for teachers with high satisfaction. The brief does not study text adaptation, so read it as context about a stretched workforce.

The cost you feel first is quality. A rewrite that drops a key term can leave students unable to follow the next lesson. A rewrite that keeps the difficulty but hides the support leaves readers stuck in the same place. Students also notice when a text feels too young for them.
Why teachers keep rewriting texts for lower reading levels

Most classes hold readers at very different levels. In a 2018 Thomas B. Fordham Institute survey, 62% of upper-elementary teachers taught at students' reading level rather than grade level. More than half of middle school teachers did the same. Adapting is the normal response in many rooms, not a fringe habit.

The national numbers show the same pressure. On the 2024 NAEP reading assessment, 40% of fourth graders performed below the NAEP Basic level, and that share was larger than in 2022. Students in that group often need more support. Teachers reach for simpler texts as one tool among several.

items: Wide gaps in one room. Some students decode well but lack background. Others struggle to decode at all.
Grade-level text that stalls readers. A passage can look fine on paper and still block a student.
Tight time. Planning, grading, and parent email already fill the week.
Tools that promise a level but cannot guarantee one. This is where many teachers get burned.

blocks.text: The first three are planning problems. The last one is a tool problem, and it is where many teachers get burned. The sections below cover the research, the free fixes, and the checks that protect your students.
What the research says about leveled texts and simpler versions

The evidence here is contested, so be careful with any strong claim, including this one. Shanahan, who wrote Leveled Reading, Leveled Lives in 2025, argues there is not strong experimental evidence that reading achievement rises when students read at their individual level. As reported by Hechinger Report, he also says simpler texts, written by people or AI, do not by themselves improve reading ability.

He argues that the critique applies mainly from second grade on. He also says students often gain from challenging text with explicit instruction. That is a secondhand account, and reviewers contest his critique. No controlled trial of teacher-adapted texts turned up in this research. So a simpler copy may not help on its own. Pair it with teaching that makes the hard parts visible.
Free fixes you can use this week

None of these fixes needs a paid tool. Apple's built-in features, a free checker, and your own reading get you most of the way. Each fix targets one failure, so match it to the problem you saw in your last rewrite.
Measure the original before you change it

Start with a number, even a rough one. In Microsoft Word, readability statistics show a Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, which Microsoft describes as a U.S. school grade. An 8.0 means an eighth grader can understand the text. Microsoft recommends about 7.0 to 8.0 for most documents, and Flesch Reading Ease scores of 60 to 70 are typical for standard files.

On a Mac, Microsoft's older-version path is Word > Preferences > Spelling & Grammar. Tick Check grammar with spelling and Show readability statistics under Grammar. Then run Review > Spelling & Grammar. Microsoft 365 on the Current Channel uses Home > Editor > Document stats instead, so check which path your copy shows.

blocks.title: A grade is a flag
blocks.text: A readability score is an estimate. It cannot tell you whether a student knows the topic or whether a rewrite kept the facts. Check both by hand before anything reaches a student.
Rewrite in passes, not in one go

Most rewrites fail because people change everything at once. Split the work into passes. In the meaning pass, state each main claim in your own words and mark the facts that must stay. In the sentence pass, shorten long sentences and put the subject near the verb. In the vocabulary pass, keep the key terms and add a short plain gloss the first time each one appears.

items: Copy the original into a new Pages or Google Docs file. Never overwrite the source.
Write each main claim in your own words. Mark every name, date, number, and key term.
Rewrite one sentence at a time. Aim for one idea per sentence where you can.
Swap rare words for plain ones. Keep the marked terms.
Run the readability check again and compare the grade with your first reading.
Read the draft aloud with Speak selection, then compare it with the original line by line.

blocks.text: Work in [Pages](/for/teachers/pages) or [Google Docs](/for/teachers/google-docs) with the original open in a second window. Keep both files. The source is your proof if a student or parent asks what changed.
Listen with Speak selection

Clumsy sentences hide on screen. Hearing them makes them easier to catch. Open Apple menu > System Settings > Accessibility > Read & Speak, then turn on Speak selection. The default shortcut is ⌥Esc. Select the rewrite, press ⌥Esc, and listen for the places where you run out of breath.

If nothing is selected, the Mac reads the text of the current window. The Info panel lets you choose word, sentence, or both highlighting, so you can follow along. You can also set a custom shortcut there if ⌥Esc clashes with another app.
Keep the original and add support

A simpler copy is one tool, not the whole plan. Keep the original text and give students support for it. Bold the key terms, add a short glossary, and offer a read-aloud version. Ask one question before reading and one after. Students then see the real text, and the hard parts are visible.

Word's Immersive Reader can help with the look of a page. On Mac it offers Column Width, Page Color, Text Spacing, Syllables, and Read Aloud. It has no Line Focus on Mac and no reading-level setting. Microsoft's educator guide names no studies, so treat the tool as a layout aid, not proof of learning.
A worked example of a reading-level rewrite

Take one sentence from a science passage: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose. That sentence packs a process, a term, and a result into one clause. Here is one way to split it, with the reason for each change.

rows: Original
Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose.
One long clause with a process, a term, and a result
Pass 1, meaning
Plants use light to make sugar. The sugar stores energy.
Kept the claim and named the result in plain words
Pass 2, sentences
Plants use light energy. They turn it into chemical energy.
Split one clause into two short sentences
Pass 3, vocabulary
Photosynthesis is how plants make food from light. The food is glucose, a kind of sugar.
Kept the term, added a gloss, and named the sugar
blocks.caption: Each pass changes one thing, so you can see what moved the level.

blocks.text: Notice what did not change. The term stayed, and so did the claim. A rewrite that drops the term can leave students unable to read the next chapter. The gloss lets a reader keep the word and still follow the sentence.
Check the rewrite before students see it

Check every rewrite against the original, line by line. Research on machine rewrites shows why. In one arXiv study, researchers rewrote 100 educational materials to a target readability level using GPT-3.5, LLaMA-2 70B, and Mixtral 8x7B. Few-shot prompting improved level control and information preservation.

The same study found that LLaMA-2 70B hit the target range more often, and GPT-3.5 kept meaning better. Manual inspection still found generated content that introduced misinformation. Edits were spread unevenly across the text. The abstract gives no match or error rates, so do not read a percentage into it.
A fluent wrong sentence is harder to catch than a clumsy one. Look for invented dates, changed numbers, and softened claims. Compare every fact with the source before you print the handout.
Where Lazur helps with reading-level rewrites

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It can explain a sentence, point at a control, and draft text. It does not click buttons, edit your files, or operate other apps for you.

For this job, Lazur works best as a second reader. Open the original and your draft, hold ⌥⌘, and ask what a sentence means in plain words. Lazur explains it out loud, so you hear the gap before a student does. Ask for a simpler draft when you want one, then check it against the source yourself.

Dictation is another honest use. Hold fn to dictate clean text at the cursor in any app. Add class vocabulary to the personal dictionary so those words come out spelled right. Snippets help with the standard glossary line you paste often.

Be clear about the limits. Lazur does not know your students, and it cannot tell you that a text fits one reader. It does not replace your reading of the child. Mistakes that make reading-level rewrites worse

items: Simplifying the ideas along with the words. Keep the claim, and cut only the clutter.
Trusting one score. A grade estimate is a flag, not a finish line.
Rewriting from memory. Memory drops facts, and that is where errors creep in.
Skipping the read-aloud. Rhythm problems show up when you hear the text.
Sending a simpler copy without the original. Students should see the real text too.
Pasting student work into a tool your school has not approved.

blocks.text: Student data and AI tools: check the rules first

Student names, work samples, and IEP details are records. Follow your school or district rules before you paste any of them into an AI tool. Use a sample passage or a public article when you test a new method. For IEP-related drafting, see [how to draft IEP goals faster](/for/teachers/problems/draft-iep-goals-faster-special-education).

Lazur sends audio and the screenshot to AI providers only while you hold the shortcut, so it can answer you. Those are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. That does not make a tool approved for your school. Your district decides that.
Your next step

Pick one passage this week and run the routine once. Time it, then compare the result with your usual method. Note what changed, what students asked, and where the draft drifted from the source. Keep the routine that saves time and still protects the meaning.

If you want the same routine for family messages, the [reply to parent emails](/for/teachers/problems/reply-parent-emails-quickly-teachers) guide covers the Gmail side. You can also [download Lazur](/download) and try the Mac features above.

faq.question: Does Lazur rewrite a text to a set reading level?
faq.answer: Lazur can draft a simpler version when you ask, and it can explain sentences out loud. Lazur's listed features do not include a readability score. Ask for a draft, then check it against the original and run your own readability check before you share it.

faq.question: What reading level should I aim for?
faq.answer: Microsoft recommends about 7.0 to 8.0 for most documents. That is a default for documents, not a rule for your class. Pick the level by reading the student's work and by the goal of the lesson. Use the score only to see whether your rewrite moved the right way.

faq.question: Is Flesch-Kincaid accurate enough to trust?
faq.answer: Treat it as a rough flag. Readability formulas are imprecise, so two texts with the same grade can read very differently. Pair the score with a read-aloud check and a look at the key terms. Your own reading of the text still decides whether it works.

faq.question: Does Immersive Reader change the reading level on Mac?
faq.answer: No. Immersive Reader offers Column Width, Page Color, Text Spacing, Syllables, and Read Aloud on Mac. It has no Line Focus on Mac and no reading-level setting. Microsoft's educator guide names no studies, so use it as a layout aid.

faq.question: Is leveled reading proven to work?
faq.answer: Not in the way many people assume. Shanahan argues there is not strong experimental evidence that reading rises when students read at their individual level. Reviewers contest his critique. Keep the original, add support, and watch what happens in your room.

faq.question: Can I paste student work into an AI tool?
faq.answer: Check your school or district rules first. Use sample passages when you test a method. Lazur sends audio and the screenshot to AI providers only while you hold the shortcut, and they are not stored. Your school may still forbid a specific tool.

faq.question: How much does Newsela cost?
faq.answer: A Common Sense Media review, last updated October 26, 2022, lists Newsela Pro at $18 per student. Prices change, so check Newsela's own pricing page before you buy. The review also says each article comes at five reading levels, roughly third through 12th grade.

costs.title: Hours you cannot get back
costs.text: Rewriting one passage is slow work. You reread the original, change a sentence, then check that the meaning survived. Multiply that by each reading group and the prep time grows fast. No source in this research measures how long adapting takes, so your own timing is the best data you have.

causes.text: A passage can look fine on paper and still stall a reader. Long sentences, rare words, and unfamiliar background all add load. Adults often miss how much a sentence asks until a student stops on it. Adapting is a response to that gap, and the gap is real.

Microsoft describes its Flesch-Kincaid grade as a U.S. school grade, which is the right way to hold it. Teachers who trust one number can produce texts that pass the score and still fail the reader.

He also argues that simpler texts do not by themselves improve reading ability. Reviewers contest that critique. Teachers hear two messages at once: match the text to the reader, and challenge the reader with hard text.

causes.title: AI rewrites read smoothly and still drift
causes.text: A fast rewrite reads well, which hides its errors. In one arXiv study of 100 educational materials rewritten to a target level, few-shot prompting improved level control and information preservation. Manual inspection still found misinformation, and edits were spread unevenly. A teacher who skips the check ships the error.

fixes.title: Measure the original first
fixes.text: Run readability statistics on the original before you change a word. In Word, the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level gives a rough U.S. school grade. Microsoft suggests about 7.0 to 8.0 for most documents. If you do not have Word, use a checker you trust and note which one you used. Then judge the text by reading it aloud.

fixes.title: Rewrite in passes
fixes.text: Do the meaning pass first, then the sentence pass, then the vocabulary pass. Mixing them makes you lose track of the claim. Each pass is short, so you can stop after any one of them. A rewrite done in passes is easier to check than one written in a single rush.

fixes.title: Keep the source open beside the draft
fixes.text: Put the original and the rewrite in two windows side by side. Mark names, dates, numbers, and key terms in the original before you start. After the rewrite, check each mark against the draft. This takes minutes, and it catches the errors that matter most.

fixes.title: Listen before you print
fixes.text: Turn on Speak selection in Apple menu > System Settings > Accessibility > Read & Speak. Then select the draft and press ⌥Esc. Listen for sentences that run too long or repeat words. Fix those first. Hearing the text catches rhythm problems that a score misses.

fixes.title: Keep the original and add support
fixes.text: Share the original with a glossary, bolded key terms, and one question before and after reading. Students then work on the real text with help. The research this page cites argues that a simpler copy alone may not build reading skill, so support matters as much as the grade.

fixes.title: Use free teacher tools with school permission
fixes.text: The MagicSchool free plan costs $0 and includes 80+ teacher tools, according to its pricing page. Check with your school before you use any AI tool with student work. Try the free plan on sample texts first, and read every output as you would a draft from a colleague.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Pick one passage and time yourself
plan.text: Choose one passage your class reads this week. Time how long a rewrite takes you with your usual method. Write the time down. You need a baseline before you can judge whether the routine saves you time.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Measure and mark the original
plan.text: Run readability statistics on the original in Word, or use a checker you trust. Mark names, dates, numbers, and key terms. Those marks are your rules for the rewrite, so keep them visible while you work.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Rewrite in passes
plan.text: Do the meaning pass first, then the sentence pass, then the vocabulary pass. Keep the original open beside the draft. Stop after each pass and reread the claims, not only the words.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Listen and check every mark
plan.text: Select the draft and press ⌥Esc to hear it with Speak selection. Fix every sentence that stumbles. Check each marked fact against the original, one by one, before you move on to the next passage.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Test with students and compare
plan.text: Use the rewrite with one group and the original with supports for another, if your school allows it. Compare the time you spent and the questions students asked. Keep what helped, and drop what did not.
